evidence.quote: In his seminal work from 1988, Nick Littlestone studied the optimal mistake bound in online learning an hypothesis class H by deterministic learning rules in the realizable setting (Littlestone, 1988); that is, under th…
In Section C.3.2 we gave two examples showing that both inequalities can be tight.
A notable example is the celebrated Multiplicative Weights (MW) learning rule, whose learning rate depends on T.
Theorem 8 implies that the adaptive procedure nearlypreserves the form of this upper bound,  guaranteeing a slightly larger ⋆ p bound of the form k + O ⋆ ⋆ k L(H) log(k log L(H)) + L(H) .
At first, the setting of prediction using expert advice looks similar, but not identical, to our setting.
Recall that we model a randomized learner as a learner which makes a “soft” prediction p ∈ [0, 1]; if the true label is y, then the learner’s loss is |p − y|.

evidence.section: F ILMUS H ANNEKE M EHALEL M ORAN
evidence.quote: Brânzei and Peres (2019) have the state-of-the-art bounds in the regime k ≪ log n, but we are not aware of any results in other regimes, e.g. when k = Θ(log n).
The upshot of this approach is that it allows for a precise combinatorial characterization of the optimal mistake bound via a natural generalization of the Littlestone dimension.

evidence.section: F ILMUS H ANNEKE M EHALEL M ORAN
evidence.quote: On the one hand, learning rules show which hypothesis classes lend themselves to learning, and on the other hand, strategies for the adversary put limitations on what can be learned, and at what cost.
